extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers (early- to mid-career) applying for competitive grants
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice and lessons learned for preparing, submitting, and presenting academic research grant proposals (with examples from ERC, NWO, Vidi, Aspasia). Focuses on proposal design, matching funder priorities, interview preparation, and responding to rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance innovation with feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The ERC emphasizes innovation balanced with feasibility, pushing applicants out of their comfort zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovation is prized but must be credible and feasible; pushing too far can provoke tough scrutiny at interview. Aim to propose novel ideas while ensuring they are plausible and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology must be well-understood and defensible
rubrics_metrics.description: “I was taking a huge gamble with the methodology that I proposed...the data analyst in the room dissected every bit of my methodology. In hindsight, I was offering something that I didn’t know enough about.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not propose methods you cannot robustly defend. Expect domain specialists on panels to probe technical details; if you lack deep expertise in a method, either gain it or avoid relying on it as the proposal's centerpiece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match proposal to the funder’s priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The NWO is much less focused on the innovation angle, and more on solid research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the funding instrument that aligns with your project's strengths (e.g., ERC values high innovation; NWO favors solidity). Adapt wording, emphasis, and possibly scope of the proposal to the specific scheme (ERC, Vidi, Aspasia, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for a high-pressure interview environment and panel scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: “The surroundings of the interview feel like they are set up to make you nervous: all applicants need to arrive at the same time...and there is a big clock behind you when you are presenting...the panel would have loved it, or there would be someone in the room who would be able to kill it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and rehearse for the stressful logistics (waiting room, visible clock) and aggressive Q&A. Practice concise presentation, anticipate critical questions (including technical critiques), and prepare to defend methodological and conceptual choices under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use feedback constructively to revise and resubmit or seek alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Aline reworked her ERC proposal and submitted it to other NWO schemes; she adapted her proposal based on feedback and ultimately found success with a different funding avenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reviewer feedback as objective input about a project, not a personal judgment. Revise proposals based on criticism, consider alternative funding schemes or formats, and resubmit when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not take rejection personally; interpret it as a judgement of the project
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s important to not take rejection personally. It is a judgement of a project rather than the researcher.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain resilience: setbacks are integral to research and can lead to unexpected opportunities. Learn from failures, avoid demoralization, and persist with improved applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider career-stage appropriateness and non-research benefits of grants
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vidi is meant for more experienced researchers who want to develop their own line of research; the Aspasia grant is awarded to female researchers with excellent proposals and offers teaching buyouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select schemes that fit your career stage and needs; weigh non-research advantages (e.g., teaching buyouts, prestige) when choosing which calls to target or accept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place innovation where it is safest (theoretical vs methodological innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I should have stayed on the safe side with my methodology and should have innovated in my theoretical model.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a novel methodological approach would be risky to defend, consider innovating in theoretical framing or other aspects of the proposal instead. Distribute novelty across dimensions to minimize fatal vulnerabilities during review.
